questions.question: 1. Which statement about a singly linked-list node is correct?

answers.a: It normally contains data and a link to the next node
answers.b: It must contain previous and next links
answers.c: It must contain its position index
answers.d: It must contain the total list size

explanations.a: Correct. A singly linked-list node normally stores data and a link to the next node.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A previous link is not required in a singly linked list.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A node does not need to store its position explicitly.
explanations.d: Incorrect. The total list size is not required in every node.

questions.question: 2. A list contains 5 → 8 → 12 → NULL. If `head` points to 5, what data is in `head->next`?

explanations.a: Incorrect. 5 is the data in the first node.
explanations.b: Incorrect. 12 is in the third node.
explanations.c: Incorrect. NULL marks the end link, not the data in the second node.
explanations.d: Correct. `head->next` refers to the second node, whose data is 8.

questions.question: 3. Which statement about memory allocation for linked-list nodes is correct?

answers.a: All nodes must be consecutive in memory
answers.b: Nodes can be allocated at different locations and connected using links
answers.c: Only the first node needs memory
answers.d: Linked lists cannot use dynamic allocation

explanations.a: Incorrect. Linked-list nodes do not have to occupy consecutive memory locations.
explanations.b: Correct. Nodes may be stored at different memory locations and connected through their links.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Every existing node requires storage.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Dynamic allocation is commonly used to create linked-list nodes.

questions.question: 4. What is the worst-case time complexity of deleting the last node when only a head pointer is available?

explanations.a: Incorrect. A head pointer does not directly identify the predecessor of the last node.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Singly linked-list traversal is not logarithmic.
explanations.c: Correct. The list may need to be traversed to locate the last node and its predecessor.
explanations.d: Incorrect. A single traversal does not require quadratic work.

questions.question: 5. Why is insertion at the beginning of a singly linked list $O(1)$ when `head` is available?

answers.c: The last node is found first
answers.d: Only the new node and a constant number of links need updating

explanations.a: Incorrect. Linked-list insertion does not require shifting existing nodes.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Existing nodes need not be traversed for head insertion.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The last node is irrelevant to insertion at the head.
explanations.d: Correct. The new node is linked to the current first node and the head reference is updated.

questions.question: 6. Which statement about a circular linked list is true?

answers.a: The last node points to NULL in every implementation
answers.b: The last node can link back to the first node
answers.c: Every node must have a previous pointer

explanations.a: Incorrect. A circular link closes the cycle instead of terminating with NULL.
explanations.b: Correct. In a circular singly linked list, the last node links back to the first node.
explanations.c: Incorrect. A previous pointer is not required for circularity.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Circular lists can be traversed sequentially with an appropriate stopping condition.

questions.question: 7. If a pointer to the node at position $k$ is already available, what is the complexity of inserting a node immediately after it?

explanations.a: Correct. Only a constant number of link assignments is required when the insertion node is already known.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Traversal is unnecessary when the required node is already referenced.
explanations.c: Incorrect. The operation does not use a logarithmic search.
explanations.d: Incorrect. Constant-time pointer updates do not require quadratic time.

questions.question: 8. A singly linked list contains $n$ nodes. If it is traversed once from head to the end, how does the running time grow with $n$?

explanations.a: Incorrect. The traversal visits nodes, so work increases with list size.
explanations.b: Incorrect. A complete sequential traversal is not logarithmic.
explanations.c: Correct. A single traversal visits each of the $n$ nodes once, so the growth is linear.
explanations.d: Incorrect. One traversal does not perform a quadratic number of visits.

questions.question: 9. Which operation is generally more convenient in a doubly linked list when a pointer to the target node is already available?

answers.d: Deleting the target without first searching for its predecessor

explanations.a: Incorrect. A previous link does not make arbitrary-value searching constant time.
explanations.b: Incorrect. Counting nodes still requires traversal.
explanations.c: Incorrect. Finding a minimum in an unsorted list requires examining nodes.
explanations.d: Correct. The previous and next links allow neighboring nodes to be updated directly when the target is already known.
